headline: Calling a 25bp RBA hike in September to 4.35%, driven by a trifecta of hawkish data: record-high trimmed mean CPI, resilient household spending, and rising discretionary consumption
reasoning: Prashant Newnaha revised his view to call a September RBA rate hike to 4.35% (actually stated as 4.6% in the transcript context) following three hawkish developments: (1) the RBA minutes showed staff recommended pre-emptive action for the first time; (2) July CPI trimmed mean hit a record high month-on-month and year-on-year, with housing CPI — rents plus cost of new dwellings — also at a record high and historically a strong lead indicator; (3) household spending rose for the third consecutive month, including discretionary spend, while the savings rate also increased, indicating consumer resilience. He views the combination of data as making it 'highly unlikely' the RBA can remain on hold.
quote: So I mean, if you have a look at the development since the start of last week, there's been a trifecta of hawkish developments. So firstly, it really started off with the uh RBA minutes on Tuesday. Uh, and while the board had decided to keep the cash rate on hold, reaching that decision by consensus, there was a hawkish element within those minutes. And that was essentially where the staff, RBA staff had actually recommended to the board that there could be the case for pre-emptive action. And that's the first time that we've actually heard the RBA talk about pre-emptive action.
episode_title: TD Securities calls for September rate hike

headline: Expects Australian bond yields to head higher and AUD to strengthen on the back of the September hike and pricing of further tightening; CapEx boom and tight labour market support the positive AUD view
reasoning: If the RBA hikes in September, markets will begin pricing in further potential tightening, pushing Australian bond yields higher. This tightening dynamic, combined with a CapEx boom and a tight labour market, should be positive for the Australian dollar. The recipe is in place for the RBA to potentially hike further, reinforcing the constructive AUD view even as higher bond yields represent an offsetting cost for fixed income holders.
quote: So obviously I think, you know markets will be, you know, pricing in the potential for the RBA to follow up with another hike. Um, so we should see bond yields heading higher on the back of that. And you know that should be positive for the Aussie dollar as well. Um, I think, you know, there's a CapEx boom taking place in Australia as well. At the moment the labor market is tight. Um, and, you know, the recipe and the ingredients are there for the RBA to potentially hike further. So it's going to be positive for the Aussie dollar. But it does mean that bond yields do head higher as well.
episode_title: TD Securities calls for September rate hike

headline: November follow-up hike not base case; would require another strong CPI print and lower unemployment — more likely any second hike comes in early next year
reasoning: While a September hike is now the central call, a November follow-up is possible but not the base view. The RBA itself expects no further hikes in its central forecast, so any additional move would be a significant deviation. The board will want to assess the lagged impact of prior hikes before acting again. If another hike does materialise, Newnaha believes it is more likely to come in early 2024 than November 2023, requiring confirmation from both a strong CPI print and a falling unemployment rate.
quote: I think we need to get another very strong CPI print, uh, and we'd need to get some jobs data showing not only is there being strong month on month increases in employment, but we probably need the unemployment rate to have lower as well. I mean, the RBA has been quite clear and they've said that, you know, the the impacts of the previous hikes have not been felt yet. So I think that the RBA will want to assess the impact of that... I think it's highly likely that it will be at the start of next year rather than at the end of this year.
episode_title: TD Securities calls for September rate hike

headline: Oil prices likely to grind higher as US Middle East intervention fails and sanctions return, pushing inflation expectations up
reasoning: Newnaha argued that the US military incursion into the Middle East has been a failure, and the US administration appears to be reverting to a sanctions-based approach. This creates a geopolitical gridlock with no clear resolution, meaning oil supply is constrained and prices are likely to drift higher. Higher oil prices are a key upside risk to inflation expectations globally and for Australia in particular, which could ultimately force the RBA's hand.
quote: I think the risk is that oil prices continue to drift higher, and that pushes inflation expectations up as well. I mean, the US excursion into the Middle East has been a failure, if anything. And it looks like the US administration is going to be returning to sanctions. Uh, and what that means is that we're essentially going to be in gridlock, um, going going ahead. So that means that oil prices are likely to grind higher, as there's no real resolution on on that front.
episode_title: Bond yields bite...or is the fear overblown?

headline: Global bond yield fears overblown relative to history; equities supported by strong earnings even if yields drift higher
reasoning: Newnaha acknowledged that bond yields are at 20-year highs in Japan, the US, and Europe, but argued the fear is overblown. When ten-year yields are measured relative to cash rates, they are not at historic highs, and the current environment is more reminiscent of pre-GFC conditions that markets were able to absorb. Earnings across commodities and other sectors remain strong, providing support for equities. However, he flagged that if the US 30-year yield breaks above 5.5%, markets would need to pay materially more attention.
quote: I think the concerns are a bit overblown at the moment. I mean, if you have a look at ten year yields across global markets relative to cash rates, we're not at historic highs. So you know there is room for yields to move higher. I'm not too concerned. If anything we're moving back to a scenario where markets were pre the GFC. Um so you know markets were able to absorb that. You have a look at the earnings... earnings are strong not just across the commodity space but across other sectors as well. So I think, you know, in terms of implications for broader broader markets like equities, it looks like the earnings story's supportive for that market. Um and even if yields do move higher um there is that support for equities. But obviously, you know if we start breaking some big levels. So the US 30 year if we start going above 5.5 then I think you know markets are going to start um paying a bit more attention to what's going on in the bond market.
episode_title: Bond yields bite...or is the fear overblown?

headline: TD Securities expects RBA on prolonged hold as conflicting forces offset each other, with hiking bias retained as optionality
reasoning: Newnaha interpreted RBA Governor Bullock's messaging as jawboning rather than a genuine hiking signal, noting the decision to cut was unanimous (9-0). The RBA's central forecast is to hold, but the governor avoided signalling hiking is off the table entirely. Domestically, weakness in the housing market and its read-through to consumption is being offset by AI-driven CapEx investment. Given these conflicting forces, TD Securities expects a prolonged hold, though markets are pricing in potential hikes if inflation expectations re-accelerate.
quote: So our view is that the RBA is going to be on a prolonged hold, uh, given these conflicting forces, but the market is obviously pricing in the potential that the RBA might need to hike again.
episode_title: Bond yields bite...or is the fear overblown?

headline: Australian wages data for Q2 came in below RBA forecasts, reducing near-term inflation pressure from the labour market
reasoning: Q2 wages data printed at 3.2% versus the RBA's forecast of 3.3%, and the Q1 figure was also revised lower to 3.2% from 3.3%. Newnaha noted this suggests no emerging inflation pressures from the labour market, which gives the RBA more time to assess incoming data, particularly from global risks such as the Middle East conflict. The jobs data for July (consensus ~12,000, TD at +15,000) was seen as unlikely to shift market pricing for a hike.
quote: The Q2 print actually came in at 3.2. So it actually missed the RBA's expectations to the downside. And also the Q1 print was also lowered as well. So annual was at 3.3 and that was lowered to 3.2. So it does look like there are no emerging inflation pressures at least coming through from the from the labor market.
episode_title: Bond yields bite...or is the fear overblown?

headline: AI-driven CapEx investment acting as a domestic demand offset to RBA-induced housing weakness in Australia
reasoning: Newnaha identified two competing forces in the Australian domestic economy: housing market weakness (with a clear read-through to household consumption) and strong AI-related capital expenditure inflows. The RBA is aware of the housing-to-consumption transmission channel and expects some pullback in consumption. The AI CapEx story is partially offsetting this drag, leaving the net economic picture unclear and justifying a wait-and-see stance from the central bank.
quote: In terms of the domestic economy, I think, you know, we've got two parts to it. We've got obviously, the housing market, which is starting to show signs of weakness, and the RBA's very well aware that the housing market has got a clear read through into consumption. So the RBA is expecting household consumption to come off somewhat. But then offsetting that, you've got a lot of investment coming in from the CapEx story on AI. So they're sort of offsetting one another.
episode_title: Bond yields bite...or is the fear overblown?
